newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serb leader urges a Zagreb-Belgrade deal.
newsitem.headline: Serb leader urges a Zagreb-Belgrade deal.

text.p: A Serb leader said on Sunday the idea of holding a referendum in the Croatian enclave of Eastern Slavonia had been scrapped and urged Zagreb and Belgrade to avert a Serb exodus from the area by striking a deal.

"All Serbs would stay in Eastern Slavonia if Yugoslavia were to conclude a double citizenship agreement with Croatia," Vojislav Stanimirovic, the head of Serb authorities of Eastern Slavonia, told Belgrade independent BK television.
Croatian laws allow for dual citizenship but Serbia has not given its citizens the option.
Eastern Slavonia will be reintegrated with the rest of Croatia after communal elections on April 13.

The Serbs are upset at Croatian plans to split the U.N.-administered Danube River region into two counties, fearing the division will deny them any local electoral majorities. They had decided to hold a referendum on the issue.
The Serbs' demand for a single district has been rejected as untenable by the Croatian government and by a U.N. Security Council statement on the enclave's future.
"The Serbs have for now given up plans for a referendum on a single administrative county because their decision would not be binding," Stanimirovic said.

Croatian state officials and media attacked the referendum plan as a stalling manoeuvre by die-hard Serb nationalists to divert attention from Zagreb's guarantees of wide-ranging minority rights for the Serb population.

Zagreb's guarantees are designed to allay Serb fears of retribution for the bloodshed in the region during the six-month war in 1991 which devastated the oil-rich fertile plain and expelled thousands of Croats from the area.

The U.N. administration (UNTAES) expects up to 20 percent of the 120,000-odd Serbs will flee to nearby Serbia rather than accept restoration of Croatian authority. Serb leaders anticipate 50 percent or more will go.

Stanimirovic said the Serbs have not yet decided whether to vote in April elections and their decision will depend largely on whether UNTAES chief Jacques Klein grants their demands. He did not specify the demands.
Western diplomats say the Serbs stand to gain electoral majorities in up to 10 of some 30 municipalities but only if they turn out to vote in significant numbers.
Stanimirovic said that there were up to 200,000 Serbs in Eastern Slavonia of whom some 100,000 are indigenous.
The rest were refugees from other enclaves which Croatia overran in offensives in 1995.
Croatia has issued about 40,000 citizenship papers to Serbs in the region, he said.
"If the Serbs decided to remain, only 25 percent Croats would return," he said.
